summary: An April 1st joke RFC proposing that the IETF raise money by selling protocol field naming rights, associating commercial brands with fields. It describes a mock process for assigning rights. It is informational and not meant seriously.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st satire imagines companies paying to put their brands in protocol field names. It sketches a mock process for reviewing and selling those names.

questions: selling naming rights in ietf protocols
did the ietf ever sell naming rights
what are protocol field naming rights
subtitle: An April 1st satire proposing that companies buy naming rights to protocol fields.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke suggests a new revenue source for the IETF: selling commercial branding rights for protocol field names.
tldr.mechanism: It imagines a process involving applications, taste review, auctions or negotiation, leases, and branded versions of RFCs.
tldr.outcome: The document is satire about commercialization and protocol naming, not a real naming-rights program.

today: RFC 5241 is an Informational April 1st satire proposing protocol field naming rights. The proposal describes a fictional branding process.

sections.title: The Branding Proposal
sections.content:
The RFC proposes that commercial brands be associated with protocol fields as a source of revenue for the IETF. It compares the idea with naming rights in sports and notes that field names are important in protocol design.

Under the imagined rule, future IETF activity and documentation would use the complete branded field name. The exaggerated consequence is part of the April 1st humor.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC jokes that a protocol field could carry a sponsor's brand. It imagines everyone having to use the full branded name.

sections.title: Taste, Pricing, and Leases
sections.content:
The proposed process would review names for taste and reject names that could confuse readers. An individual or organization could apply for a field, present a proposed brand, and negotiate a lease term.

The memo considers auctions and negotiation for pricing and suggests using an existing dispute policy. Its examples pair protocol field names with commercial brands and deliberately absurd combinations.
sections.plainLanguage: The imagined market has applications, a taste review, prices, and time-limited leases. The proposed examples make clear that the process is a joke.

sections.title: Imagined Changes to IANA and RFC Publishing
sections.content:
The memo proposes an IANA Protocol Branding Catalog mapping fields to brand names and lease dates. It also imagines converting RFCs to XML and producing “Real_RFC” copies with branded field names inserted.

Tool builders would update xml2rfc to consult the catalog. The RFC concludes that the proposal has costs but could provide revenue, keeping its satire in a formal standards-document style.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke imagines a database and software that would add brand names to RFCs. The detailed administrative plan is part of the parody.
